patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.complaint: Left cheek pain and thick green nasal discharge for 12 days after a cold
background: Penicillin allergy: widespread rash as a teenager

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with facial pain, purulent discharge and blocked nose after a cold, or 'Which is the most likely complication?' when the eye swells or a headache becomes severe.

points: Priya, 34, had a **cold** two weeks ago.
Now: throbbing pain over her **left cheek**, worse bending forward.
Thick **green nasal discharge** and a blocked nose.
Food tastes of nothing; she **cannot smell** her coffee.
She felt better on day 5, then **worse again**.

steps.lead: Priya's cold inflamed her nose and sinuses; a second worsening after a viral start hints at **secondary bacterial** infection.
Priya has three risk factors in one: a **recent URTI**, **allergic rhinitis** and **smoking**. Her left cheek pain points to the **maxillary** sinus.

visual.title: Priya's symptoms since the cold
visual.caption: Better, then worse again ('double sickening'), lasting beyond 10 days: suspect bacterial rhinosinusitis.

points: Pressing over her left maxilla is **tender**.
Anterior rhinoscopy: **pus** in the left nasal cavity.
Eyes normal: no swelling, full movements, normal vision.

steps.lead: Every classic feature is here: **facial pain**, purulent discharge, congestion, loss of smell, and **maxillary tenderness** with pus seen in the nose.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Priya?
steps.r: Facial pain with **purulent discharge, congestion and anosmia** after a cold is rhinosinusitis. Cluster headache and migraine have no discharge; a dental abscess gives tooth pain.

steps.title: Facial pain: rhinosinusitis vs the look-alikes
head: Feature
Rhinosinusitis
Dental abscess
Cluster headache

steps.lead: Priya's eyes and neurology are normal, so there are **no red flags** for orbital or intracranial spread today.
Her sinuses sit right next to her **orbit** and **brain**: that is why she is safety-netted for eye swelling or a severe headache.

steps.text: A swollen, red eyelid with **painful or reduced eye movements** in sinusitis is **orbital cellulitis**, not simple conjunctivitis. It needs same-day hospital assessment.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical diagnosis), or CT sinuses when disease is severe, recurrent or complicated.

steps.q: Priya asks whether she needs an X-ray or a scan. What confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: Acute rhinosinusitis is a **clinical diagnosis**. Imaging and swabs do not change management in uncomplicated cases.

steps.lead: Priya's history and examination make the diagnosis: **no blood tests, swab or imaging** are needed today.

visual.title: How long have symptoms lasted?
visual.label: Priya 12 days
visual.caption: Priya is acute. Symptoms beyond 12 weeks make it chronic rhinosinusitis.

steps.lead: If Priya's sinusitis kept coming back or became severe, **CT sinuses** would show the anatomy, blocked ostia and any polyps.

steps.text: Plain **sinus X-rays** are not used. If imaging is needed, it is **CT sinuses**; a suspected orbital or intracranial complication needs urgent contrast CT.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' where the duration and severity decide: self-care first, intranasal steroid for moderate symptoms, and phenoxymethylpenicillin (doxycycline if allergic) beyond 10 days or if severe.

visual.title: Days of symptoms
visual.label: Priya day 12
visual.caption: Priya has crossed the 10-day line and worsened after improving.

steps.lead: Priya already takes **paracetamol and ibuprofen**. Her symptoms are moderate, so she starts **intranasal fluticasone** and saline irrigation.

steps.q: Priya's symptoms have lasted 12 days and worsened. She is penicillin allergic. Which antibiotic?
steps.r: Beyond 10 days, the first-line antibiotic is **phenoxymethylpenicillin**; with a penicillin allergy it is **doxycycline** (clarithromycin is the alternative).

steps.lead: Priya qualifies for an antibiotic (**over 10 days**). Because of her penicillin allergy she gets **doxycycline** instead of phenoxymethylpenicillin.

steps.title: Acute rhinosinusitis pathway
nodes: Red flags (eye, neuro, severe headache)? → urgent hospital assessment
Up to 10 days → self-care: paracetamol, ibuprofen
steps.caption: Red flags first; then the 10-day line decides antibiotics.

steps.lead: Priya's plan follows **NICE NG79**: no antibiotic in the first 10 days, then a narrow-spectrum antibiotic if symptoms persist or are severe.
Priya does not need ENT now. If she developed **chronic** symptoms with **polyps**, a deviated septum, or **one-sided** pain or bleeding, she would be referred.

steps.text: **One-sided** chronic nasal symptoms (blockage, bleeding, pain) need ENT referral to exclude a structural cause or **tumour**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the maxillary sinus is most affected, how a viral infection leads to bacterial sinusitis, or how infection reaches the orbit.

steps.lead: Priya's cold swelled her mucosa and slowed her cilia; blocked **ostia** trapped mucus where bacteria could multiply.

steps.title: From cold to bacterial sinusitis
nodes: Mucosal oedema and impaired mucociliary clearance

steps.q: Why is Priya's maxillary sinus the one infected?
steps.r: The maxillary ostium is **high on the medial wall** and narrow, so it drains **against gravity** and blocks easily.

steps.lead: Priya's left maxillary sinus could not drain upwards through its narrow ostium, so secretions **pooled** and became infected.
Fluticasone shrinks Priya's swollen mucosa, **reopening the ostia** so the sinus can drain again.
Only a thin plate of bone (the **lamina papyracea**) separates Priya's ethmoid sinus from her orbit: infection can spread straight through.

steps.text: **Orbital cellulitis** in children usually comes from the **ethmoid** sinus through the lamina papyracea.

mcq.q: Which sinus is most commonly affected in rhinosinusitis?
mcq.r: The **maxillary** sinus, because its ostium drains against gravity.
Most cases are **viral**; bacterial infection often follows secondarily.

mcq.q: Which is a risk factor for rhinosinusitis?
mcq.r: Recent URTI, **allergic rhinitis** and smoking are the risk factors in the notes.

mcq.q: Which complication of rhinosinusitis presents with a swollen eye and painful eye movements?
mcq.r: Spread into the orbit causes **orbital cellulitis**.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing acute rhinosinusitis?
Which investigation is used in severe or recurrent rhinosinusitis?
mcq.r: **CT sinuses** for severe or recurrent disease.

mcq.q: After how many days of symptoms should an antibiotic be considered?
mcq.r: Symptoms persisting beyond **10 days**, or severe symptoms.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is first-line for bacterial rhinosinusitis?
Which treatment is first-line for moderate-severe symptoms?

o: Reduce mucosal oedema and improve drainage
mcq.r: They **reduce inflammation and oedema**, reopening the sinus ostia.

technique.stem: A 41 year old man has a 2 week history of pain over his right cheek and a blocked nose. It started after a cold. The pain is worse when he bends forward. He has thick yellow nasal discharge and has lost his sense of smell. There is tenderness over the right maxilla. His eyes and neurological examination are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about facial pain: look for nasal symptoms.
Post-viral onset, **purulent discharge**, anosmia and maxillary tenderness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Facial pain + purulent discharge + congestion after a cold = **acute rhinosinusitis**.

elim: Allergic rhinitis gives clear discharge, sneezing and itch, not facial pain with pus.
Cluster headache: severe periorbital attacks lasting minutes to hours, clear rhinorrhoea.
A dental abscess gives tooth pain and swelling, no nasal discharge.
Trigeminal neuralgia is seconds-long electric shocks with no discharge.

steps.x: **A. Acute rhinosinusitis.** Rule: facial pain plus purulent nasal discharge after a cold.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 6 day history of facial pain, nasal congestion and green nasal discharge following a cold. She is otherwise well. Her temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 80 bpm. There is tenderness over both maxillary sinuses. Her eyes and neurological examination are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question in a well patient: ask whether any test changes management.

clues: Her eyes and neurological examination are normal
steps.x: Short history, well, **no red flags**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis is a **clinical diagnosis**: no tests.

elim: CT sinuses is for severe or recurrent disease, or complications.
Bloods do not change management in a well patient.
MRI is not used for uncomplicated sinusitis.
Swabs are not routinely used; most cases are viral.

steps.x: **E. No investigation needed.** Rule: typical sinusitis without red flags is diagnosed clinically.

technique.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 14 day history of facial pain, nasal blockage and purulent nasal discharge after a cold. Her symptoms are not improving despite paracetamol and ibuprofen. She has no penicillin allergy. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Her eyes and neurology are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: the duration and allergy status decide.

clues: not improving despite paracetamol and ibuprofen
steps.x: Beyond **10 days**, failed self-care, not allergic, no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Persistent symptoms beyond 10 days: first-line **phenoxymethylpenicillin**.

elim: Co-amoxiclav is reserved for severe or failed first-line treatment.
Ciprofloxacin is not used for sinusitis.
Doxycycline is for penicillin allergy; she has none.
ENT is for structural problems or unilateral chronic symptoms.

steps.x: **D. Phenoxymethylpenicillin.** Rule: over 10 days, not allergic = penicillin V.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man has recurrent episodes of left cheek pain and purulent nasal discharge after colds. CT sinuses shows fluid in the left maxillary sinus, while the frontal and ethmoid sinuses are clear.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason the maxillary sinus is affected?
o: It has the largest number of goblet cells
It is lined by squamous epithelium

steps.x: A mechanism question: why this sinus?

clues: fluid in the left maxillary sinus
frontal and ethmoid sinuses are clear
steps.x: Only the maxillary sinus has pooled secretions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The maxillary ostium is **high and narrow**, draining **against gravity**, so secretions stagnate.

elim: Goblet cell number is not the explanation.
Sinuses are lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium, not squamous.
It has a good blood supply.
Wall thickness does not explain stasis; thin walls explain spread.

steps.x: **D. Its ostium drains against gravity.** Narrow, upward drainage = obstruction and stasis.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 12 day history of a blocked nose, thick green nasal discharge and pain over both cheeks. She had a cold before this started and felt better for a few days before getting worse. She has reduced sense of smell. Her temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Both maxillae are tender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Worsening after initial improvement, symptoms beyond 10 days, purulent discharge and maxillary tenderness point to bacterial rhinosinusitis. A cold resolves in about a week.

steps.x: Diagnosis: viral cold versus sinusitis versus allergy.

clues: felt better for a few days before getting worse
steps.x: Beyond 10 days, **double sickening**, purulent discharge, sinus tenderness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Secondary bacterial infection after a viral start: **acute bacterial rhinosinusitis**.

elim: Allergic rhinitis: clear discharge, sneezing, itch, no fever.
A cold settles within about a week and does not worsen again.
Migraine has no purulent discharge or sinus tenderness.
Polyps give chronic blockage and anosmia, not acute pain and pus.

steps.x: **A. Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis.** Better then worse beyond 10 days = bacterial.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has facial pain and nasal congestion after a cold. He describes pressure under his right eye extending to his upper teeth. He has purulent nasal discharge.
practice.q: Which sinus is most likely to be affected?
practice.e: Pain in the cheek under the eye radiating to the upper teeth is the maxillary sinus, the most commonly affected. Frontal gives forehead pain; sphenoid gives deep or vertex headache.

steps.x: Which sinus: map the pain to the anatomy.
Cheek pain spreading to the upper teeth = **maxillary**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **maxillary** sinus sits above the upper teeth roots and is the most common.

elim: Ethmoid pain is between the eyes.
Frontal pain is over the forehead.
Mastoid air cells relate to the ear, not the nose.
Sphenoid gives deep, retro-orbital or vertex headache.

steps.x: **C. Maxillary.** The commonest sinus; pain under the eye and into the upper teeth.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has recurrent facial pain and purulent nasal discharge every few months. She has seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes each summer and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor for her rhinosinusitis?
practice.e: Seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes are allergic rhinitis, a key risk factor (with smoking and recent URTI) because it causes chronic mucosal oedema.

steps.x: A risk factor question: which option is in the notes' list?
Hay fever pattern = **allergic rhinitis**; smoking is also a risk but is not an option.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Risk factors: recent URTI, **allergic rhinitis**, smoking.

elim: Asthma is not described here.
Female sex is not a recognised risk factor.
Iron deficiency does not predispose to sinusitis.
The pill is not a risk factor.

steps.x: **A. Allergic rhinitis.** Swollen mucosa blocks the ostia.

practice.stem: A 9 year old boy has had a cold with purulent nasal discharge for 8 days. Today his left eyelids are red and swollen, and moving the left eye is painful. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Left eye movements are reduced.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Eyelid swelling with painful and reduced eye movements after sinusitis is orbital cellulitis, from spread through the lamina papyracea. A brain abscess gives headache and neurological signs.

steps.x: A complication question: where has the sinus infection gone?

clues: moving the left eye is painful
steps.x: Sinusitis followed by eye signs: **painful, reduced movements** mean the orbit is involved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Spread into the orbit: **orbital cellulitis**, an emergency.

elim: Allergic conjunctivitis is itchy with normal eye movements and no fever.
Brain abscess gives headache, vomiting or focal neurology.
Dacryocystitis is a swelling at the medial canthus over the tear sac.
Eczema is not febrile and does not restrict eye movement.

steps.x: **D. Orbital cellulitis.** Sinusitis + painful, reduced eye movements = orbital spread.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has a 10 day history of sinus pain and purulent nasal discharge. Over 2 days he has developed a severe headache, vomiting and confusion. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. He has a right-sided weakness. There is no neck stiffness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Sinusitis followed by severe headache, fever, confusion and focal weakness is intracranial spread: a brain abscess. Orbital cellulitis affects the eye, and SAH is sudden-onset without a preceding infection.

steps.x: Complication question: the new features tell you where infection has spread.

clues: sinus pain and purulent nasal discharge
steps.x: Red flags: severe headache and **focal neurology** after sinusitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Intracranial spread through the skull base: **brain abscess**.

elim: Chronic sinusitis is 12+ weeks of symptoms, not acute neurology.
Migraine does not cause fever, raised CRP and confusion.
Orbital cellulitis gives eye swelling and painful eye movements.
SAH is a thunderclap headache with no preceding sinus infection.

steps.x: **A. Brain abscess.** Sinusitis + headache + neuro signs = intracranial complication.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has had a cold for 5 days. She now has facial pressure and a blocked nose. A medical student examines her.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination if she has maxillary rhinosinusitis?
practice.e: Maxillary sinusitis causes tenderness over the affected sinus and purulent discharge in the nasal cavity. Pale boggy turbinates and clear rhinorrhoea suggest allergic rhinitis.

steps.x: A finding question: what would you see or feel in maxillary sinusitis?
The sinus is under the cheek.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tenderness over the maxillary sinus** (cheek), with purulent discharge in the nose.

elim: Red eyes suggest conjunctivitis or allergy.
Clear discharge fits a cold or allergy; sinusitis is purulent.
Pale, boggy turbinates are allergic rhinitis.
Tonsillar exudate is tonsillitis.

steps.x: **D. Tenderness over the cheek.** Tender sinus + pus in the nose.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man has a 4 day history of nasal congestion, facial pain and yellow nasal discharge after a cold. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. There is tenderness over the left maxilla. His eyes and neurological examination are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute rhinosinusitis is a clinical diagnosis, the gold standard in the notes. CT sinuses is reserved for severe or recurrent disease.

steps.x: Confirming the diagnosis: what is the gold standard?

clues: eyes and neurological examination are normal
steps.x: Short, uncomplicated, no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clinical diagnosis** from history and examination.

elim: CT is for severe or recurrent disease, or complications.
MRI is not used for uncomplicated sinusitis.
Swabs are not routine and most cases are viral.
Plain X-rays are not used.

steps.x: **A. Clinical assessment.** Rhinosinusitis is a clinical diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has had five episodes of rhinosinusitis in the last year, each needing antibiotics. Between episodes she has a persistently blocked nose. Her temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Recurrent rhinosinusitis needs CT sinuses to look for anatomical obstruction or polyps. Plain X-rays are not used.

steps.x: Investigation in recurrent disease: second-line imaging.

clues: five episodes of rhinosinusitis in the last year
steps.x: **Recurrent** disease with persistent blockage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe or recurrent: **CT sinuses**.

elim: Allergy testing may help but does not show sinus anatomy.
A swab does not explain why it keeps recurring.
Recurrent disease warrants imaging.
Plain X-rays are not used for sinus disease.

steps.x: **B. CT sinuses.** Recurrent or severe = CT.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has a 5 day history of facial pain, nasal congestion and purulent discharge after a cold. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 122/80 mmHg. His eyes and neurology are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Within 10 days and well, management is self-care with paracetamol and ibuprofen. Antibiotics are for symptoms beyond 10 days or severe disease.

steps.x: Initial management: check the day count.
Under 10 days, mild, no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Likely viral: **self-care** with paracetamol and ibuprofen.

elim: Doxycycline is for penicillin-allergic patients needing antibiotics.
Oral steroids are only for intense flares.
Antibiotics wait until beyond 10 days or severe symptoms.
ENT is for structural or unilateral chronic problems.

steps.x: **C. Paracetamol and ibuprofen.** Under 10 days = self-care.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has a 13 day history of facial pain and purulent nasal discharge that is getting worse despite paracetamol, ibuprofen and fluticasone nasal spray. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. Her eyes and neurology are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: Beyond 10 days with penicillin allergy, doxycycline is first choice (clarithromycin the alternative). Amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin and penicillin V are all penicillins.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: check the allergy.
Beyond 10 days and worsening, with a **true penicillin allergy**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Penicillin allergic: **doxycycline**.

elim: Amoxicillin is a penicillin.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin and targets skin staph.
Penicillin V is first-line only if not allergic.

steps.x: **C. Doxycycline.** Allergic = doxycycline (or clarithromycin).

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has 5 months of a blocked left nostril, left-sided facial pain and occasional blood-stained discharge from the left side. The right side is clear. He has tried a fluticasone nasal spray without benefit. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: Unilateral chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with pain and bleeding need ENT referral to exclude a structural cause or tumour. More medical treatment would delay this.

steps.x: Next step: is this a referral situation?

clues: blood-stained discharge from the left side
steps.x: **Chronic**, **one-sided**, with bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unilateral chronic symptoms = **ENT referral**.

elim: Steroids treat flares but miss a structural cause.
Antibiotics do not address a chronic unilateral problem.
Reassurance is unsafe with unilateral bleeding.
Decongestants cause rebound and delay diagnosis.

steps.x: **D. Referral to ENT.** One-sided chronic symptoms = refer.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman develops facial pain and purulent nasal discharge 10 days after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. A swab later grows Streptococcus pneumoniae.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism allowing bacterial infection to develop?
o: Mucosal oedema blocking the sinus ostia
practice.e: Viral infection causes mucosal oedema and impaired mucociliary clearance, blocking the ostia so secretions stagnate and bacteria multiply.

steps.x: Mechanism: how does viral become bacterial?

clues: 10 days after a viral upper respiratory tract infection
steps.x: A viral start, then a secondary bacterial infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oedema and impaired clearance **obstruct the ostia**: stasis lets bacteria grow.

elim: Bacteria need stasis, not invasion of intact mucosa.
Sinusitis is not spread from the blood or lungs.
Mucociliary clearance is impaired, not increased.
Mucus secretion increases.

steps.x: **D. Mucosal oedema blocking the sinus ostia.** Blocked drainage = stasis = infection.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: viral first, bacterial second; maxillary most often.

points.p: Inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses
points.why: The 'rhino' part: the nose is always involved too.
So antibiotics are not needed in the first 10 days.
Double sickening suggests the bacterial phase.

prompts.q: Name the risk factors for rhinosinusitis.

points.why: Chronic mucosal oedema blocks the ostia.

Severe headache, fever, confusion, focal signs.

prompts.q: How is rhinosinusitis diagnosed, and when is imaging used?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: most stems want 'no investigation'; recurrent or severe wants CT.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis is the gold standard
CT sinuses for severe or recurrent disease
points.why: Plain sinus X-rays are not used.

points.p: Urgent imaging if orbital or intracranial complication suspected

prompts.q: Walk through the treatment of acute rhinosinusitis, from mild to severe.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 10-day line and the allergy status decide the answer.

points.why: First 10 days: most cases are viral.

points.p: Moderate-severe: intranasal corticosteroid (fluticasone) with saline irrigation
points.why: Reduces oedema and opens the ostia.
Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and under 12s.

prompts.q: When should a patient with rhinosinusitis be referred to ENT?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'one-sided' in a chronic stem is the referral trigger.

prompts.q: Why does a viral infection lead to bacterial sinusitis, and why is the maxillary sinus most affected?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: oedema, cilia, blocked ostium, stasis.

points.p: Obstructed ostia allow secondary bacterial infection
Maxillary ostium drains against gravity and is narrow
points.why: It sits high on the medial wall.

prompts.q: How do intranasal steroids work, and how does sinus infection reach the orbit and brain?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: thin bone is the route for spread.

points.p: Direct spread through thin bony walls
Lamina papyracea (to orbit) and skull base (to brain)

glossary.Rhinosinusitis: Inflammation of the nasal lining and the paranasal sinuses together.
glossary.Paranasal sinuses: Air-filled spaces in the facial bones (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid) that drain into the nose.
glossary.Maxillary sinus: The largest sinus, in the cheekbone under the eye; the one most often infected.
glossary.Ethmoid sinus: Small air cells between the eyes, separated from the orbit by very thin bone.
glossary.Frontal sinus: Sinus in the forehead bone above the eyebrows.
glossary.Sphenoid sinus: Deep sinus behind the nose, near the pituitary and cavernous sinus.
glossary.Ostium: The small opening through which a sinus drains into the nose.
glossary.Ostia: Plural of ostium: the drainage openings of the sinuses.
glossary.Mucociliary clearance: The sweeping of mucus out of the airways and sinuses by beating cilia.
glossary.Cilia: Tiny hair-like projections on lining cells that beat to move mucus.
glossary.Mucosal oedema: Swelling of the lining of the nose and sinuses from inflammation.
glossary.Purulent: Containing pus, so thick and yellow or green.
glossary.Anosmia: Loss of the sense of smell.
glossary.Anterior rhinoscopy: Looking into the front of the nose with a light and speculum.
glossary.Double sickening: Getting better from a cold and then worse again, suggesting secondary bacterial infection.
glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection: an infection of the nose, sinuses, throat or larynx.
glossary.Allergic rhinitis: Hay fever: allergic inflammation of the nose with sneezing, itch and clear discharge.
glossary.Orbital cellulitis: Infection of the tissues behind the orbital septum, causing painful, reduced eye movements; an emergency.
glossary.Periorbital cellulitis: Infection of the eyelid skin in front of the orbital septum, with normal eye movements.
glossary.Lamina papyracea: The paper-thin bone between the ethmoid sinus and the orbit.
glossary.Brain abscess: A collection of pus within the brain, causing headache, fever and focal neurology.
glossary.Nasal polyps: Soft, painless swellings of the nasal lining that block the nose and reduce smell.
glossary.Deviated septum: A nasal septum bent to one side, narrowing one nostril.
glossary.Saline irrigation: Rinsing the nose with salt water to wash out mucus.
glossary.Fluticasone: An intranasal corticosteroid spray that reduces nasal and sinus inflammation.
glossary.Intranasal corticosteroid: A steroid spray into the nose that reduces mucosal swelling.
glossary.Phenoxymethylpenicillin: Penicillin V: the first-line oral antibiotic for bacterial sinusitis.
glossary.Doxycycline: A tetracycline antibiotic used when a patient is penicillin allergic; avoid in pregnancy and young children.
glossary.Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic, an alternative in penicillin allergy.
glossary.Xylometazoline: A decongestant nasal spray; causes rebound congestion if used for more than a week.
glossary.CT sinuses: A CT scan of the facial sinuses, used in severe, recurrent or complicated disease.
glossary.NG79: The NICE guideline on antibiotic prescribing for acute sinusitis.
